what-is-artificial-intelligence: AI = computers doing tasks that normally need human thinking.
Machine learning = learning patterns from examples instead of writing every rule.
Deep learning = machine learning with neural networks of many layers.
Generative AI = creates new text, images or code.
Every system today is narrow AI: very good at some tasks, not a general thinking mind.
AI can be wrong. Check anything that matters.
math-and-statistics-for-ai: A vector = a list of numbers. AI turns words, pictures and data into vectors.
Similarity: how close two vectors are. Search by meaning is built on it.
Probability = how likely each outcome is. A language model scores every possible next word.
Loss = a number for how wrong the model was.
Gradient descent = change the model a little in the direction that lowers the loss, and repeat.
machine-learning-basics: Three ways to learn: supervised (with answers), unsupervised (find groups), reinforcement (rewards).
Split data: training set (learn), validation set (compare settings), test set (final honest check).
Keep the test set locked away until the end.
Overfitting: great training score, poor test score. The model memorised.
Underfitting: the model is too simple to learn the pattern.
Accuracy is not enough. Look at precision and recall too.
deep-learning-and-transformers: A neuron is a small calculator. Many layers learn more complex patterns.
Training: guess, measure the loss, adjust the weights, repeat.
Your words become tokens, then embeddings (lists of numbers carrying meaning).
Attention lets each word look at the others and decide which matter.
At the end the model scores every possible next token and picks one.
introduction-to-generative-ai: Predictive AI picks a label or a number. Generative AI creates new content.
A foundation model is trained once on a very large amount of data and used for many tasks.
Core idea: predict the next piece (word, pixel, sound).
Output can be fluent and still wrong (hallucination).
A person must check anything that matters. Use it responsibly.
how-large-language-models-work: The prompt is split into tokens (words or parts of words).
The context window is how many tokens the model can read at once.
The model scores every possible next token. Sampling picks one.
Low temperature = safest choices. High temperature = more varied.
Each new token is fed back in and the loop repeats.
The model predicts likely text. It does not look facts up, so it can sound sure and be wrong.
llm-architecture-and-optimization: Parameters = the numbers a model learned. Large models have billions.
They take a lot of memory. Memory needed is roughly parameters times bytes per parameter.
Quantization stores numbers with fewer bits: a smaller model, a small loss in quality.
Inference = running the model to answer. GPUs do many calculations in parallel.
Long chats get expensive because the cache and the context grow.
prompt-engineering-basics: Say clearly what the task is. A vague prompt gets a vague answer.
Give a role, the reader and the length.
Add context the model cannot know: your text, data or rules.
A few examples of the exact output teach the format better than a description.
Zero-shot = no examples, one-shot = one, few-shot = several.
Reuse a good prompt as a template with variables.
advanced-prompting-techniques: One huge prompt often gives a messy answer. Split it into steps.
Prompt chaining: the output of one prompt becomes the input of the next.
Ask the model to check its own draft against your rules (reflection).
Pass data between steps in a clear format, for example JSON.
Small steps are easier to test and fix than one giant prompt.
structured-outputs-json: Describe the exact shape you want: field names, types, allowed values.
Never trust the output blindly. Parse and validate every field.
Extract the JSON, check it against the schema, then repair or retry with the error message.
If it still fails, fall back to a safe default.
Only validated data reaches the rest of your app.
prompt-testing-and-security: Build a golden test set: real inputs with the answers you expect.
Save every prompt change as a new version so you can compare and roll back.
A new prompt must not make old cases fail.
Prompt injection = text in a document or message that tries to give the model new orders.
Treat outside text as data, not instructions. Never let the model alone approve risky actions.
